report:
**Conclusion: no—the claim is not supported.** Masks can reduce SARS‑CoV‑2 infections when a large share of a population wears them, but the effect depends substantially on mask quality, fit, consistent use, setting, and baseline transmission. They are a risk-reduction measure, not a guarantee against infection.

The strongest direct evidence is a large cluster-randomized trial in 600 Bangladeshi villages (342,183 adults). A program distributing masks and promoting their use increased observed mask-wearing and reduced *symptomatic, serologically confirmed* SARS‑CoV‑2 infection by about 9%; the reduction was clearer among older adults and in villages assigned surgical masks. Because villages—not individuals—were randomized, this is unusually relevant to the question of widespread community uptake. It does not show that any mask policy, mask type, or level of adherence will work equally well.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34855513/

Supporting evidence includes a CDC-reviewed body of laboratory, observational, and outbreak studies: masks provide **source control** (limit virus exhaled by infected people) and some wearer filtration; the expected community benefit rises as more people use well-fitting masks consistently. This evidence is less definitive than a fully controlled population trial because real-world studies can be confounded by other precautions and behavior.  
https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/science/science-briefs/masking-science-sars-cov2.html

A systematic review/meta-analysis also found an association between mask use and lower COVID‑19 infection risk, while explicitly noting the need for more robust randomized trials. Thus, reasonable uncertainty about the *size* of benefit remains—but “masks cannot reduce infections at high population uptake” conflicts with the best available direct trial evidence.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33347937/
